summary: This best current practice describes a simple process in which authors of Internet-Drafts add an Implementation Status section recording known implementations. That lets reviewers and working groups give proper weight to documents backed by running code, which can be evidence that a specification works.

eli5.summary: Before a recipe goes in a cookbook, it helps to know who has cooked it and how it turned out. This asks authors to list the people who have actually built what they describe.

questions: what is the implementation status section
what is rough consensus and running code
is the implementation status section mandatory
subtitle: A lightweight way for Internet-Draft authors to list who has actually implemented their protocol.

tldr.problem: Implementation is not a requirement for publishing an RFC, so reviewers often cannot tell whether a draft has running code behind it.
tldr.mechanism: Authors may add an Implementation Status section to an Internet-Draft, listing known implementations in a simple format, and ask the RFC Editor to remove it before publication.
tldr.outcome: The process is not mandatory. It advances the experiment of RFC 6982 to a Best Current Practice and obsoletes that document.

facts.label: Before publication
facts.value: Section removed by the RFC Editor

today: RFC 7942 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 205) published in July 2016, and it obsoletes RFC 6982. The unit metadata shows no later RFC obsoleting or updating it.

sections.title: Why Track Running Code
sections.content:
Many IETF participants know the saying "rough consensus and running code". Yet implementation is not a requirement for publication as an RFC, and some Proposed Standards were published without any implementation. Some may never be implemented.

Policies have varied. The Routing Area once required one or more implementations before a Proposed Standard (RFC 1264). Later that was lifted and each working group could set its own rules (RFC 4794). The Inter-Domain Routing (IDR) working group still requires two independent implementations.

The hypothesis here is that implementing a specification before publication benefits the process, for example by showing it is comprehensible and that there is enough interest to implement it.
sections.eli5: Some rulebooks get published before anyone has tried playing the game. This note says it helps to try the game first and write down who did.

sections.title: Scope and Voluntary Use
sections.content:
The process is not mandatory. Authors are encouraged to consider it, and working groups are invited to think about applying it to all their protocol specifications. Working groups decide how to use the information. One result might be that documents are processed more rapidly.

It covers all Internet-Drafts with implementable specifications, whether produced inside working groups or outside them but intended for IETF consensus. Drafts on the Independent Stream are explicitly out of scope. The greatest benefit is expected for Standards Track documents developed within working groups.

The process began as an experiment in RFC 6982, which this document obsoletes, advancing the process to a Best Current Practice.
sections.eli5: Nobody is forced to use it. It is an offer to authors, and each group decides how much to care about the answers.

sections.title: The Implementation Status Section
sections.content:
An Internet-Draft may contain a section titled "Implementation Status", placed just before "Security Considerations". For each implementation it may include some or all of: the responsible organization; the name or a link; a brief description; the maturity level (research, prototype, alpha, beta, production, widely used and so on); coverage of the specification; the draft versions implemented; licensing terms; implementation experience; contact information; and the date the entry was last updated.

The section can also cover interoperability, with references to test-case descriptions and reports. Chairs and area directors are asked to make sure it is not used as a marketing venue.

Because the information is time dependent, it is inappropriate in a published RFC. Authors should add a note asking the RFC Editor to remove the section before publication, so the RFC errata process does not apply to it.
sections.eli5: Each builder gets a little card: who they are, what they built, how finished it is and how to reach them. The cards are thrown away when the book is printed.

sections.title: The Boilerplate Introduction
sections.content:
The RFC proposes boilerplate text to head the section. It says the section records known implementations at the time of posting and is meant to assist the IETF in progressing drafts to RFCs. It states that listing an implementation does not imply endorsement by the IETF, that no effort was spent verifying contributed information, and that it is not a catalog of available implementations.

Authors are also asked to put a note to the RFC Editor at the top of the section, asking that the entire section and the reference to RFC 7942 be removed before publication.
sections.eli5: The cards start with a short warning label: we did not check these, and being listed does not mean the IETF approves.

sections.title: Alternative Formats
sections.content:
Sometimes it is better to publish implementation status separately, for example on the IETF wiki. The RFC lists these cases: the section has grown too large to manage in the document; a working group wants implementors rather than authors to keep entries current; a working group already runs an active wiki; or the information stays valuable after the draft becomes an RFC.

Readers of the draft should still be made aware of it, initially by replacing the section's contents with a URL to the wiki. If published separately, the information needs to be openly available without authentication, registration or access controls to have any useful effect.
sections.eli5: If the cards pile up, you can keep them on a shared noticeboard instead, as long as anyone can walk up and read them.

sections.title: Benefits
sections.content:
The RFC lists several benefits to a working group. Members, chairs and area directors can use the information to prioritize drafts, for instance when competing proposals exist, or to decide whether a document should move to a different track such as individual submission or Experimental. Making it public motivates participants to implement proposals, which helps find flaws early. Others can use the software to evaluate protocol features, check correctness to some degree, and look at resilience and scalability. They can also test interoperability or, with open source, study the code.

The RFC adds a caution: code should never be used in lieu of a clear specification. It does not say whether or how much working groups should prefer proposals that have running code.
sections.eli5: Knowing who built it helps everyone pick the best ideas, find mistakes early and try things out. But the written rules still come first.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: This is a process document, so it has no direct effect on the security of any particular IETF protocol. The authors add only that better-reviewed protocols are likely to also be more secure.
sections.eli5: This is a rule about paperwork, not about locks, but protocols that more people have tried tend to be safer.
